title: Alternating Current

standard_text: Alternating currents, peak and RMS value of alternating current/voltage; reactance and impedance; LCR series circuit (phasors only), resonance, power in AC circuits, power factor, wattless current. AC generator, transformer.

body_html:
How to think about it

An AC voltage V₀ sin ωt has rms value V₀/√2; Indian mains is 220–230 V rms at 50 Hz. An inductor has reactance XL = ωL and makes the current lag by 90°; a capacitor has XC = 1/ωC and makes it lead by 90°.

In a series LCR circuit Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²); at resonance XL = XC, Z = R and the current is greatest. Average power is VrmsIrms cos φ with power factor cos φ = R/Z. Transformers change voltage in the ratio of turns.

Example

V₀ = 311 V. Vrms?

311 ÷ 1.414

Answer: 220 V

Example

R = 3, XL = 8, XC = 4. Z?

√(9 + 16)

Answer: 5 Ω

Common mistakes

  • Adding XL and XC.
  • Using peak values for power.
  • Saying a capacitor passes DC.

faq.q: What happens at resonance in a series LCR circuit?
faq.a: X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>, the impedance equals R and the current is a maximum.
cos φ = R/Z, the fraction of V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub> that is actually used as power.

items.q: Why can transformers not work with DC?
c: a steady current gives no changing flux, so no e.m.f. is induced

items.q: What happens at resonance in a series LCR circuit?
c: X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>, the impedance is minimum and the current is maximum
